name: THE I AIN'T MESCLUN YOU AT ALL BURGER

recipe.history:
Mesclun — from the Provençal word 'mescla,' meaning mixture — is not a single plant but a philosophy: a carefully composed blend of young, tender salad greens chosen for their variety of flavors, textures, and colors. The tradition of mesclun originated in the Cours Saleya market of Nice, in the Provence region of southern France, where market vendors assembled daily mixtures of young leaves from the surrounding countryside for sale to restaurants and home cooks. A classic Niçois mesclun included chervil, arugula (roquette), lettuce, and endive — each contributing something distinct: the anise note of chervil, the pepperiness of arugula, the mild sweetness of lettuce, the slight bitterness of endive. The composition varied by season and by market, but the principle remained constant: variety and balance, the whole greater than the sum of its parts. Mesclun was not a commodity but a craft, assembled by someone with knowledge and taste. This tradition connected mesclun to the broader culture of Provençal cooking, which prizes freshness, seasonality, and the honest flavors of carefully grown ingredients above elaborate technique. The region's abundant sunshine and moderate climate were ideal for growing the diverse array of salad plants that went into the blend, and the tradition of consuming tender young greens was as old as the region's cultivation itself.

Mesclun arrived in the United States with a bang in the 1980s, largely through the influence of Alice Waters and the kitchen team at Chez Panisse in Berkeley, California. Waters had traveled extensively in France and had encountered mesclun in the markets of Provence; she began growing similar mixed greens on farms connected to Chez Panisse and serving the mixture, dressed simply with good vinaigrette, as a revelation to American diners accustomed to iceberg lettuce. The 'California salad' — arugula, frisée, radicchio, mâche, and baby lettuces dressed with sherry vinaigrette and perhaps some shaved Parmesan — became one of the defining dishes of the American farm-to-table movement. By the 1990s, bagged mesclun was available in mainstream supermarkets across the country, and the concept had been so thoroughly absorbed into American cooking that most diners no longer knew its French origins. On a burger, mesclun provides something that iceberg cannot: a range of flavors, from sweet to bitter to peppery, that evolves with each bite and stands up to a complex, layered vinaigrette rather than wilting under it.

The first time I dressed a serious salad — not just torn lettuce with bottled dressing, but a proper composition with mesclun, fresh herbs, shaved cheese, and a vinaigrette made from scratch — I understood something about cooking that had been opaque to me before: the dressing is not a condiment but an ingredient, and its ratio matters as much as anything else in the dish. I had been taught by a more experienced cook to dress a salad by tasting as I went: a little acid, a little oil, season with salt, taste again. The goal was not to coat the leaves but to season them — to bring out their own flavors while adding enough acid and fat to make each leaf cohesive with the others. It took me twenty minutes the first time, standing over the bowl and tasting and adjusting until the balance was right. When I finally got it, the mesclun tasted more like itself than it had before being dressed — brighter, more focused, unified. I put this dressed mesclun on a burger that night almost as an afterthought, and the result was one of those moments where an accidental discovery reorders your thinking about a dish. The dressed greens did not just garnish the burger; they became essential to it.

A properly dressed mesclun should be placed on a medium rare patty — cooked to 130–135°F — because the slight warmth of the patty gently wilts the greens just enough to integrate them with the other toppings without destroying their texture and freshness. A well-done patty runs hotter and can overwhelm tender greens, cooking them rather than merely warming them and reducing them to a soggy, uninteresting tangle. The vinaigrette on the mesclun also performs a specific function in relation to the patty: it provides acidity that cuts through the fat of the beef, refreshing the palate between bites. This function is most effective when the beef is still rich and fatty — that is, when it's medium rare. The acid and fat of the vinaigrette and the fat and juice of the patty create a back-and-forth that defines the eating experience of this burger. Cook the patty past medium rare and you eliminate one side of that conversation.
ingredients: 2 tbsp mixed seeds (sesame, sunflower, poppy) for topping
⅓ cup good-quality extra-virgin olive oil
2 tbsp fresh chervil or flat-leaf parsley, finely minced
5 oz mesclun mix (arugula, frisée, mâche, baby lettuces, radicchio, endive — whatever is freshest)
2 tbsp additional fresh herbs: chervil, tarragon, flat-leaf parsley
2 tbsp shaved Parmesan or Pecorino Romano
Herb vinaigrette (as needed to lightly coat)
For the Dijon and tarragon aioli:
Salt and white pepper to taste
½ tsp dried herbes de Provence
4 slices Brie or double-crème Brie, rind on
Fresh tarragon or chervil sprigs, for garnish
instructions: 1. Make the multigrain buns: Dissolve yeast in warm water with honey. Let stand 5–10 minutes until foamy. In a stand mixer with dough hook, combine both flours, rolled oats, flaxseeds, sunflower seeds, and salt. Add yeast mixture, olive oil, and egg. Knead on medium 8–10 minutes until smooth. The dough will be slightly dense. Place in oiled bowl, cover, and rise 1½ hours until doubled.

2. Divide dough into 6 portions, shape into balls, and place on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Cover and proof 45 minutes. Preheat oven to 375°F. Brush with egg wash and press mixed seeds on top. Bake 20–22 minutes until deep golden and hollow-sounding. Cool completely.

3. Make the herb vinaigrette: In a small bowl, combine white wine vinegar, lemon juice, Dijon, minced shallot, grated garlic, salt, pepper, and honey. Whisk until the salt dissolves. Slowly drizzle in olive oil while whisking vigorously to emulsify. Stir in all minced fresh herbs. Taste and adjust — it should be bright, herby, and balanced. The vinaigrette can be made ahead; whisk again before using.

4. Make the Dijon and tarragon aioli: Combine both Dijons, mayonnaise, minced tarragon, white wine vinegar, and grated garlic. Whisk until smooth. Season with salt and white pepper. Refrigerate until needed.
5. Form patties: Gently combine ground beef with salt, pepper, garlic powder, and herbes de Provence. Divide into 4 portions (about 6 oz each). Shape into ¾-inch-thick patties with a center dimple.

6. Cook patties: Heat a cast iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook patties 3–4 minutes on the first side without pressing. Flip. Lay Brie slices over each patty immediately after flipping. Cook 2–3 more minutes until Brie is beginning to melt and internal temperature reaches 130–135°F for medium rare. Remove and rest 3 minutes.
7. Toast buns: Melt butter in a skillet over medium heat and toast buns cut-side down 2–3 minutes until golden.

8. Dress the mesclun: Place mesclun and fresh herbs in a large bowl. Drizzle with just enough herb vinaigrette to lightly coat — start with 2 tablespoons and add more if needed. Toss gently with your hands to coat without bruising. Add shaved Parmesan. Season with a pinch of flaky salt.

9. Assemble: Spread Dijon and tarragon aioli on both cut sides of each bun. Place the medium rare patty with melted Brie on the bottom bun. If using, add a slice of heirloom tomato. Top with a generous handful of dressed mesclun, piling it high. Garnish with a sprig of fresh tarragon or chervil. Finish with flaky sea salt. Cap with the top bun and serve immediately — the mesclun should be fresh and barely wilted, not sitting.
